narrative: The model estimated a 67.4% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure more likely than success—about two chances in three—so your law school application was denied on that basis. The strongest factor was your third-year class standing: you were in the second decile, far below the roughly sixth-decile average among accepted students, and this pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year standing was the next most influential factor; also second decile versus an accepted average near sixth, it reinforced the failure prediction. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 was the third most important factor, but it pushed in the opposite direction: it is above the accepted-student average of about 3.23 and counted as evidence you could pass. It was not enough to outweigh the two class-standing signals. To move forward, ask admissions for feedback, work with academic advisors to raise your class standing in advanced law coursework, and document sustained improvement before reapplying. You may also consider retaking the LSAT or strengthening your record through additional rigorous coursework, then request reconsideration with evidence that addresses the main concern: your recent academic performance.
